p03-c2-t.name: p03-c2-t

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p03-c2-t.text:
$D_{t+1}=\|\mathbf{v}_t-\alpha\mathbf{v}^\ast +\rho_t\mathbf{s}_t\|^2=D_t+2\rho_t\mathbf{v}_t^T\mathbf{s}_t-2\rho_t\alpha\mathbf{v}^{\ast T}\mathbf{s}_t+\rho_t^2\|\mathbf{s}_t\|^2$
Apply $\mathbf{v}_t^T\mathbf{s}_t\le0$, $\mathbf{v}^{\ast T}\mathbf{s}_t\ge\gamma$, $\|\mathbf{s}_t\|^2\le B^2$
Choose $\alpha=B^2/(2\gamma)$, sum all inequalities, then look at the right side

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p03-ban-t.text: Takeaway: each update adds at most $\rho ^{2}B^{2}$ to the distance and removes at least $2\rho \alpha \gamma$.

p05-c2-t.name: p05-c2-t

p05-c2-t.text:
[Correction] The result is not that $D_t$ equals exactly 0, nor $\mathbf{v}_t=\alpha\mathbf{v}^\ast $
Nonseparable data have no strictly feasible $v^{\ast }$, so the premise fails; but failing to finish in finitely many steps does not prove the data are nonseparable
In practice, tell real numbers apart from floating-point error

p06-ctx-t.text: **Used on this page**: fixed $\rho>0$; $D_{t+1}\le D_t+\rho^2B^2-2\rho\alpha\gamma$; series conditions are sufficient, not necessary.

p06-fig-title.name: p06-fig-title

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p06-fig-title.text: Choose $\alpha$ above $\rho B^{2}/(2\gamma )$; each step removes at least $\varepsilon$

p06-c2-t.name: p06-c2-t

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p06-c2-t.text:
Take $\alpha>\rho B^2/(2\gamma)$; then $\epsilon=2\rho\alpha\gamma-\rho^2B^2>0$, and $D_{t+1}\le D_t-\epsilon$
Infinitely many updates still give a negative bound, so it must stop in finitely many steps
This proof fits this unit's finite, strictly separable batch setting, and does not claim the step must go to 0

[Added] For the four points take $\mathbf{u}=(-1,1,0)^T/\sqrt2$, $R=\sqrt2$, $\gamma_0=1/\sqrt2$, so $M\le4$

p08-bridge.name: p08-bridge

p08-bridge.text: Last page: the update-count bound. This page compares the sums of 1/t and $1/t^{2}$.

p08-ctx-t.name: p08-ctx-t

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p08-ctx-t.text: **Used on this page**: series $\sum_{t\ge1}1/t$ and $\sum_{t\ge1}1/t^2$; start at $t=1$, integral test; do not plug in $t=0$.

p08-fig-title.name: p08-fig-title

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p08-fig-title.text: Problem: of the first 40 partial sums, which keeps growing?

p08-c2-t.name: p08-c2-t

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p08-c2-t.text:
Integral test: $\int_1^\infty dt/t=\infty$, so $\sum1/t$ diverges; $\int_1^\infty dt/t^2=1$, so $\sum1/t^2$ converges
So $\rho_k=1/(k+1)$ satisfies $\sum\rho_k=\infty$ and $\sum\rho_k^2<\infty$
[Added] The limit of $\sum1/t^2$ is about 1.645 (the first 40 terms give about 1.62)

p08-bx3-t.text: Next question: can we correct without waiting for the whole batch?

steps.label: Goal: prove by contradiction that… · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes: Goal: prove by contradiction that… · 1/3 · Female: The batch update from the last unit sometimes succeeds at once and sometimes needs many rounds. Think: will it always stop? This unit proves it: if the data are finite and strictly separable, it stops after finitely many steps.

narration.label: s1.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The batch update from the last unit sometimes succeeds at once and sometimes needs many rounds. Think: will it always stop? This unit proves it: if the data are finite and strictly separable, it stops after finitely many steps.

steps.label: Goal: prove by contradiction that… · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Goal: prove by contradiction that… · 2/3 · Male: The route is a proof by contradiction. Step one: assume the updates never stop. Step two: expand the squared distance to a feasible target. Step three: add up the inequality from each update. Step four: a nonnegative distance turns out smaller than a negative number, a contradiction.

narration.label: s2.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: The route is a proof by contradiction. Step one: assume the updates never stop. Step two: expand the squared distance to a feasible target. Step three: add up the inequality from each update. Step four: a nonnegative distance turns out smaller than a negative number, a contradiction.

steps.label: Goal: prove by contradiction that… · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Goal: prove by contradiction that… · 3/3 · Female: Take this away: if infinitely many updates made the distance negative, the infinite assumption fails. Next page, we meet the four quantities the proof uses.

narration.label: s3.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Take this away: if infinitely many updates made the distance negative, the infinite assumption fails. Next page, we meet the four quantities the proof uses.

steps.label: Four quantities: feasible… · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes: Four quantities: feasible… · 1/3 · Male: First, four quantities. The feasible weights v star make every labeled score positive, with minimum gamma. The total correction direction s is the sum of y times a over the mistakes, with squared length at most B squared. Think: what sign does v star times s have?

narration.label: s4.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: First, four quantities. The feasible weights v star make every labeled score positive, with minimum gamma. The total correction direction s is the sum of y times a over the mistakes, with squared length at most B squared. Think: what sign does v star times s have?

steps.label: Four quantities: feasible… · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Four quantities: feasible… · 2/3 · Female: When the set is nonempty, each mistake contributes at least gamma, so v star times s is at least gamma. On the other hand, a mistake's labeled score is at most zero, so the current weights times s are at most zero. These two inequalities are the core of the proof.

narration.label: s5.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: When the set is nonempty, each mistake contributes at least gamma, so v star times s is at least gamma. On the other hand, a mistake's labeled score is at most zero, so the current weights times s are at most zero. These two inequalities are the core of the proof.

steps.label: Four quantities: feasible… · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Four quantities: feasible… · 3/3 · Male: Take this away: when the set is nonempty, the total correction is at least gamma against v star and at most zero against the current weights. Next page, we expand the squared distance.

narration.label: s6.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: Take this away: when the set is nonempty, the total correction is at least gamma against v star and at most zero against the current weights. Next page, we expand the squared distance.

steps.label: Squared distance: each update… · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes: Squared distance: each update… · 1/3 · Female: Substitute the update into the squared distance and expand it into four terms. Predict: which term is obviously not positive?

narration.label: s7.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Substitute the update into the squared distance and expand it into four terms. Predict: which term is obviously not positive?

steps.label: Squared distance: each update… · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Squared distance: each update… · 2/3 · Male: The second term, 2 rho times v t times s, because v t times s is at most zero, so we can drop it. The third term, minus 2 rho alpha times v star times s, shrinks the distance by at least 2 rho alpha gamma. The fourth term, rho squared times the squared length of s, is at most rho squared B squared.

narration.label: s8.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: The second term, 2 rho times v t times s, because v t times s is at most zero, so we can drop it. The third term, minus 2 rho alpha times v star times s, shrinks the distance by at least 2 rho alpha gamma. The fourth term, rho squared times the squared length of s, is at most rho squared B squared.

steps.label: Squared distance: each update… · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Squared distance: each update… · 3/3 · Female: Take this away: each update adds at most rho squared B squared to the distance and removes at least 2 rho alpha gamma. Next page, we add these inequalities up.

narration.label: s9.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Take this away: each update adds at most rho squared B squared to the distance and removes at least 2 rho alpha gamma. Next page, we add these inequalities up.

steps.label: Summing:   diverges and   ^{2}… · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes: Summing:   diverges and   ^{2}… · 1/3 · Male: In the figure, the blue line is the bound if the updates never stop. It starts at 8 and falls slowly as updates grow. Note this is a series sketch, not a real training run. Guess when it drops below zero.

narration.label: s10.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: In the figure, the blue line is the bound if the updates never stop. It starts at 8 and falls slowly as updates grow. Note this is a series sketch, not a real training run. Guess when it drops below zero.

steps.label: Summing:   diverges and   ^{2}… · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Summing:   diverges and   ^{2}… · 2/3 · Female: At t equal 5 the bound is about 6.08; at t equal 80 about 1.31; and after about 157 updates it turns negative. Because the sum of rho diverges while the sum of rho squared converges, the right side must end up negative, but the squared distance on the left cannot be negative.

narration.label: s11.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: At t equal 5 the bound is about 6.08; at t equal 80 about 1.31; and after about 157 updates it turns negative. Because the sum of rho diverges while the sum of rho squared converges, the right side must end up negative, but the squared distance on the left cannot be negative.

steps.label: Summing:   diverges and   ^{2}… · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Summing:   diverges and   ^{2}… · 3/3 · Male: Take this away: a nonnegative distance cannot be below zero, so updates cannot continue forever. Next page, we clarify what this proves.

narration.label: s12.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: Take this away: a nonnegative distance cannot be below zero, so updates cannot continue forever. Next page, we clarify what this proves.

steps.label: Myth: proving it stops means… · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes: Myth: proving it stops means… · 1/3 · Female: A common myth: since it is proved to stop, does it end exactly at that feasible target? Think: is there only one feasible line?

narration.label: s13.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: A common myth: since it is proved to stop, does it end exactly at that feasible target? Think: is there only one feasible line?

steps.label: Myth: proving it stops means… · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Myth: proving it stops means… · 2/3 · Male: No. The proof does not say the distance equals zero, nor that the weights equal the target, since feasible lines are usually not unique. It only guarantees that after finitely many updates, the mistake set is empty.

narration.label: s14.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: No. The proof does not say the distance equals zero, nor that the weights equal the target, since feasible lines are usually not unique. It only guarantees that after finitely many updates, the mistake set is empty.

steps.label: Myth: proving it stops means… · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Myth: proving it stops means… · 3/3 · Female: Take this away: the proof guarantees stopping, not stopping at one particular line. Also, for nonseparable data the premise fails, but a failed training run does not prove the data are nonseparable. Next page, a fixed learning rate.

narration.label: s15.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Take this away: the proof guarantees stopping, not stopping at one particular line. Also, for nonseparable data the premise fails, but a failed training run does not prove the data are nonseparable. Next page, a fixed learning rate.

steps.label: A fixed rate also stops: place… · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes: A fixed rate also stops: place… · 1/3 · Male: The two series conditions above are sufficient, not necessary. If the learning rate is fixed, does the proof still work? Predict: which quantity do we change?

narration.label: s16.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: The two series conditions above are sufficient, not necessary. If the learning rate is fixed, does the proof still work? Predict: which quantity do we change?

steps.label: A fixed rate also stops: place… · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: A fixed rate also stops: place… · 2/3 · Female: We choose a farther analysis target, with alpha greater than rho times B squared over 2 gamma. Then epsilon, equal to 2 rho alpha gamma minus rho squared B squared, is positive, and each update reduces the distance by at least epsilon.

narration.label: s17.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: We choose a farther analysis target, with alpha greater than rho times B squared over 2 gamma. Then epsilon, equal to 2 rho alpha gamma minus rho squared B squared, is positive, and each update reduces the distance by at least epsilon.

steps.label: A fixed rate also stops: place… · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: A fixed rate also stops: place… · 3/3 · Male: Infinitely many updates still give a negative bound, so it must stop in finitely many steps. Take this away: with a fixed rate, every update reduces the distance by at least a fixed amount. Next page, another bound on the number of updates.

narration.label: s18.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: Infinitely many updates still give a negative bound, so it must stop in finitely many steps. Take this away: with a fixed rate, every update reduces the distance by at least a fixed amount. Next page, another bound on the number of updates.

steps.label: Going deeper: the four-point… · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes: Going deeper: the four-point… · 1/3 · Female: The going-deeper version is the per-sample update. In the figure, two blue positives, two orange negatives, and the purple arrow is the direction u. Each point times its label has inner product 1 over root 2 with u, and that is gamma zero.

narration.label: s19.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The going-deeper version is the per-sample update. In the figure, two blue positives, two orange negatives, and the purple arrow is the direction u. Each point times its label has inner product 1 over root 2 with u, and that is gamma zero.

steps.label: Going deeper: the four-point… · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Going deeper: the four-point… · 2/3 · Male: The longest point has length root 2, and that is R. After M corrections, the length along u is at least M rho gamma zero, and the total length is at most rho R root M. Cancel rho, and M is at most R over gamma zero, squared, which here is 4.

narration.label: s20.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: The longest point has length root 2, and that is R. After M corrections, the length along u is at least M rho gamma zero, and the total length is at most rho R root M. Cancel rho, and M is at most R over gamma zero, squared, which here is 4.

steps.label: Going deeper: the four-point… · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Going deeper: the four-point… · 3/3 · Female: Take this away: the bound 4 is only a guarantee; only 2 corrections actually happen. Note this bounds the number of corrections, not the number of sweeps, and it cannot be applied directly to the batch formula.

narration.label: s21.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Take this away: the bound 4 is only a guarantee; only 2 corrections actually happen. Note this bounds the number of corrections, not the number of sweeps, and it cannot be applied directly to the batch formula.

steps.label: Practice: compare the infinite… · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes: Practice: compare the infinite… · 1/3 · Male: Your turn. Compare the infinite series of 1 over t and 1 over t squared, starting at t equal 1; do not plug in t equal zero. The figure shows the first 40 partial sums. Guess: which one keeps growing?

narration.label: s22.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: Your turn. Compare the infinite series of 1 over t and 1 over t squared, starting at t equal 1; do not plug in t equal zero. The figure shows the first 40 partial sums. Guess: which one keeps growing?

steps.label: Practice: compare the infinite… · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Practice: compare the infinite… · 2/3 · Female: Use the integral test. The integral of 1 over t is infinite, so it diverges. The integral of 1 over t squared equals 1, so it converges. That is exactly the step size's two conditions: the sum of rho diverges and the sum of rho squared converges.

narration.label: s23.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Use the integral test. The integral of 1 over t is infinite, so it diverges. The integral of 1 over t squared equals 1, so it converges. That is exactly the step size's two conditions: the sum of rho diverges and the sum of rho squared converges.

steps.label: Practice: compare the infinite… · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Practice: compare the infinite… · 3/3 · Male: Take this away: one infinite sum diverges and one converges, matching the step size's two conditions. The next question: can we correct without waiting for the whole batch? The next unit covers the online perceptron.

narration.transcript: Male: Take this away: one infinite sum diverges and one converges, matching the step size's two conditions. The next question: can we correct without waiting for the whole batch? The next unit covers the online perceptron.
